title: API 653 Training in Philadelphia: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for Philadelphia tank inspectors: Delaware River terminals, refinery tank fields and Chapter 245 work, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 653 Training in Philadelphia: Exam Preparation for Aboveground Storage Tank Inspectors on the Delaware River
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors in and around Philadelphia

Storage is a large share of Delaware Valley inspection work. A chemical and ethanol terminal sits on the Port Richmond waterfront, crude and products tanks fill the refinery yards at Trainer, Paulsboro and Delaware City, and Pennsylvania builds API 653 methods into its own tank regulation, which keeps certified inspectors busy. This page is for tank technicians, MFL and UT floor-scan crews, terminal staff, tank construction and repair workers and engineers who want API 653 certification.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia. The API 653 course is studied online at your own pace, and an instructor answers questions about API 653, API 650 and the other documents in the Body of Knowledge as you go. The American Petroleum Institute sets eligibility under Annex D of API 653, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification; the course prepares you for that exam but grants nothing itself, and Atlantis holds no API training-provider approval.

Philadelphia’s tank farms, from Port Richmond to Tinicum

  • Kinder Morgan, Philadelphia terminal. The company’s terminal sheet describes 35 acres on North Delaware Avenue with 100 tanks from 119 to 100,000 barrels, about 1.19 million barrels in all, handling chemicals and ethanol. It lists nitrogen blanketing, product heating and vapour recovery, a ship dock and a barge dock, and rail access from CSX and Norfolk Southern. PhilaPort’s Tioga liquid bulk berth next door connects with the same tank farm.
  • Energy Transfer, Fort Mifflin terminal. In Tinicum Township, Delaware County, this former crude receiving terminal is inactive, according to a DEP permit fact sheet from early 2025, which also notes that the site hydrostatically tests aboveground tanks as part of regulatory compliance inspections when needed. Idle tanks still need an inspection plan.
  • Refinery tank fields. Monroe Energy at Trainer and PBF at Paulsboro and Delaware City all run large tank fields for crude, intermediates and products. PBF calls Paulsboro the largest asphalt producer on the East Coast, and it describes the neighbouring CPI site as marine, railcar, asphalt and storage infrastructure, so heated asphalt tanks are part of the local picture.
  • Upriver in Bucks County. Kinder Morgan’s Fairless Hills terminal is mainly a bulk and breakbulk port, but its sheet lists a 150,000-barrel liquid storage tank, a reminder that single large tanks turn up at sites that are not tank terminals.

Terminal tanks change product more often than refinery tanks, and the Kinder Morgan list of chemicals and ethanol is a good example of why an inspector has to ask what a tank holds now, what it held before and whether the change of service needs an evaluation under API 653.

Tanks around Philadelphia that are not API 653 tanks

API 653 is written for aboveground atmospheric tanks built to API 650 or its predecessor API 12C. Two large local storage systems fall outside that core. At Marcus Hook, Energy Transfer’s fact sheet describes new chilling and refrigerated storage, six tanks built since 2013 holding about 3 million barrels of propane, ethane and butane, and an existing 2 million barrels of underground cavern storage. Liquids this light can only be held in large atmospheric tanks if they are refrigerated. In the city, Philadelphia Gas Works stores liquefied natural gas at its Passyunk plant, which a 2018 Kleinman Center analysis described as having a 250 MMcf LNG storage tank. Refrigerated tanks like these are built to low-temperature tank standards such as API 620 and API 625, and pressurised spheres and bullets for gas liquids are pressure vessels inspected under API 510.

The distinction matters twice. On the exam, a question about an API 620 or pressure-storage scenario will not be answered from API 653’s rules. On the API application, experience on refrigerated or pressurised storage should be described accurately, because API decides whether it counts toward API 653.

Pennsylvania’s Chapter 245 and the DEP tank inspector certificate

Pennsylvania regulates aboveground tanks under 25 Pa. Code Chapter 245, and the inspections it requires are performed by third-party inspectors certified by the Department of Environmental Protection. The department has two inspector categories: IAM for manufactured tanks and IAF for field-constructed and manufactured tanks. Slides from DEP’s 2018 inspector seminar list what each needs: four years of experience, an application and a DEP examination, with the IAF category requiring a current API 653 certification and an attachment documenting 12 activities, and the IAM category accepting either API 653 or STI SP001 certification. Renewal requires the API 653 certification to be maintained and attendance at DEP’s technical seminar.

Two features of the rule shape careers here. First, under 25 Pa. Code 245.106 a certified inspector may not be an employee of the tank owner or operator, so Chapter 245 inspections are a third-party market. Second, the schedule is fixed in regulation. For tanks over 21,000 gallons, DEP’s guidance sets the first in-service inspection within five years of installation and later ones by API 653’s calculated service life or a quarter of the corrosion-rate life, never more than five years apart; the first out-of-service inspection comes within ten years, and later ones follow the service-life method or half the corrosion-rate life with a 20-year ceiling. An older DEP presentation adds that the bottom evaluation must use UT and visual examination plus at least one other method, such as magnetic flux testing or vacuum testing of lap welds.

An API 653 certificate on its own does not make you a DEP-certified inspector, but on DEP’s 2018 slides it is the gateway to the field-constructed category. Atlantis’s page on API 653 tank inspection in Pennsylvania describes the same regime from the owner’s side.

Across the river: New Jersey and Delaware

At New Jersey major facilities, N.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16(d) requires field-erected steel atmospheric tanks over 2,000 gallons to follow API 653 and its schedule, but not its similar-service or risk-based scheduling. In Delaware, DNREC administers its own aboveground storage tank regulation, 7 DE Admin. Code 1352, for tanks over 250 gallons holding regulated substances. A Delaware City or Paulsboro inspector therefore works to the same API 653 with a different state rule beside it.

Breakout tanks and the federal layer

Where a tank serves as a breakout tank on a hazardous liquid pipeline, 49 CFR 195.432 applies on top of any state rule. Paragraph (a) calls for an inspection of each in-service breakout tank at least once each calendar year, at intervals not exceeding 15 months, except for tanks inspected under paragraphs (b) and (c). Paragraph (b) sends atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks to API 653 and says API 653’s risk-based methods cannot be used to determine the internal inspection interval; paragraph (c) covers tanks built to API 2510 through API 510. PHMSA published a proposed rule in 2026 that would allow risk-based internal intervals with caps, but until it becomes final the current text stands. The exam tests API 653, not Part 195, yet a terminal inspector who mixes the two will make mistakes in the field.

What Delaware River service does to tank shells, floors and roofs

  • Ethanol. Fuel-grade ethanol, handled at the Port Richmond terminal, can cause stress corrosion cracking of carbon steel, which API RP 571 describes; welds and areas of high residual stress need crack-detection methods, not just thickness readings.
  • Chemicals under nitrogen. A nitrogen blanket keeps air and moisture away from the product, so internal damage depends on the chemical stored; a change of product can change the damage mechanism overnight.
  • Heated asphalt. Insulated, heated asphalt tanks bring corrosion under insulation on the shell and roof, and their roofs and vents need attention where vapours condense.
  • Idle tanks. A tank taken out of service still corrodes from the soil side and from water left behind; the return-to-service decision, including whether a hydrostatic test is needed, is an API 653 question.
  • Winter. Cold weather slows floor work and repairs, so many Delaware Valley owners schedule out-of-service inspections and floor replacements for the warmer months, and floating-roof drains need checking after hard freezes.

Worked example: projecting a floor to its next internal inspection

A products tank at a Pennsylvania terminal has just finished an out-of-service inspection and repairs. It has no release prevention barrier or other means of detecting and containing a bottom leak, so API 653 requires at least 0.10 in. of bottom plate remaining at the next internal inspection. After repairs, the lowest remaining thickness from soil-side corrosion (RTbc) is 0.205 in. and from product-side pitting (RTip) is 0.190 in. The maximum unrepaired product-side rate (StPr) is 0.003 in. a year and the soil-side rate (UPr) is 0.004 in. a year.

  1. Formula. API 653 projects the floor as MRT = (the lower of RTbc and RTip) − Or × (StPr + UPr), where Or is the years to the next internal inspection.
  2. Try 15 years. MRT = 0.190 − 15 × 0.007 = 0.085 in., below 0.10 in., so 15 years is too long.
  3. Solve for the limit. Or = (0.190 − 0.100) ÷ 0.007 = about 12.9 years, so the plan sets the next internal inspection at no more than 12 years.
  4. Check the state rule. Chapter 245 adds its own ceiling for the next out-of-service inspection; here API 653’s figure is the shorter one and governs, but on a tank with very low corrosion rates the state maximum could govern instead.

The usual exam traps are taking the higher of RTbc and RTip, forgetting that both rates act together over the interval, and using the wrong minimum when the question mentions a release prevention barrier or a lining. The API 653 practice questions page has more floor, shell and settlement problems, and the guide to settlement measurement and acceptance covers the survey side.

Becoming an API 653 inspector in the Philadelphia market

API 653’s Annex D counts experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. One year of supervising or performing tank inspection is enough with a BS in engineering or technology; two years of tank design, construction, repair, operation or inspection are needed with a two-year degree, three with a high-school diploma and five or more without formal education, in each case including a year of inspection. Local routes:

  • Floor-scan and UT technicians working for Delaware Valley tank inspection contractors, who already collect much of the data a Chapter 245 report rests on. Atlantis offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training in Philadelphia for the method side.
  • Tank construction and repair crews, including boilermakers and welders, whose repair experience counts on the longer routes; welders preparing for inspection roles may also look at AWS CWI exam prep in Philadelphia.
  • Terminal operators and maintenance staff, whose operating experience counts, although in Pennsylvania they cannot later perform the Chapter 245 inspection on their own employer’s tanks.
  • Engineers in terminal and refinery integrity groups, on the shortest route.

The full rules are on the API 653 certification requirements page; API, not Atlantis, verifies each application.

Studying API 653 with API 650 open beside it

Much of the open-book half depends on API 650, so practise moving between the two documents: shell thickness rules, hydrostatic test conditions, welding and NDE requirements for repairs, and the annexes. Use the self-paced format to work through API 653’s inspection, evaluation and repair sections during the slower winter months, when outdoor tank work in the region eases, and keep timed practice for the weeks before your window. Send the instructor the questions your own tanks raise, such as how a heated tank or a change of product should be evaluated. API 653 is sat in person, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Philadelphia.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Philadelphia terminal or inspection company

Inspection companies working the Chapter 245 market often sponsor technicians toward API 653 as the first step to DEP certification, and terminal owners sponsor their own staff for in-house programmes and repair oversight even though the state inspection must be third-party. One enquiry can cover a group in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware, each person studying on their own schedule. Fees are quoted on request, and every candidate applies to API individually.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in person in Philadelphia?
faq.a: Not from Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia, and the API 653 course is online and self-paced with instructor Q&A, so tank crews can study around the outdoor season. The examination is the in-person part: API administers it at Prometric test centres, and Prometric lists centres in and around Philadelphia.

faq.q: Do I need API 653 certification to become a Pennsylvania DEP-certified tank inspector?
faq.a: For the field-constructed (IAF) category, yes: slides from DEP’s 2018 inspector seminar list a current API 653 certification as a requirement, together with four years of experience, a record of qualifying activities and a DEP examination. The manufactured-tank (IAM) category accepts API 653 or STI SP001. Check DEP’s current requirements before you apply, because the state, not API, issues that certification.

faq.q: I work for a terminal. Can I perform the Chapter 245 inspections on my employer’s tanks?
faq.a: No. Under 25 Pa. Code 245.106 a DEP-certified inspector may not be an employee of the tank owner or operator, so the regulated inspections are performed by third-party inspectors. API 653 knowledge is still valuable inside a terminal, for planning, repair oversight and reviewing third-party reports, and terminal experience can count toward API 653 eligibility.

faq.q: Are the refrigerated storage tanks at Marcus Hook covered by API 653?
faq.a: Not as their core standard. API 653 covers atmospheric tanks built to API 650 or API 12C. Refrigerated tanks for propane, ethane and butane are normally built to low-temperature tank standards such as API 620 and API 625, and pressurised spheres and bullets are pressure vessels under API 510. Describe that kind of experience accurately on your API application.

faq.q: Which API 653 calculations should a Philadelphia candidate practise first?
faq.a: Start with the floor projection (MRT), shell minimum thickness and remaining life, and settlement evaluation, because they are both common on the exam and part of everyday Chapter 245 work. Then add hydrostatic test height and the welding and repair rules. Use the practice questions and check every answer against the code clause rather than a memorised shortcut.

faq.q: Does the API 653 exam test Chapter 245 or New Jersey’s tank rules?
faq.a: No. The examination tests API 653, API 650 and the other documents on the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your window. Pennsylvania’s Chapter 245 and New Jersey’s discharge-prevention rules decide how you work in the Delaware Valley, but an exam answer based on them will be marked wrong if it conflicts with the code.

faq.q: Can an inspection company sponsor several tank technicians on one quote?
faq.a: Yes. One enquiry can cover a group, and each technician studies at their own pace with instructor Q&A, which suits crews who travel between Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware sites. Fees are quoted on request. Each person must meet API 653’s Annex D experience rules and applies to API individually.
